verbose: I have some holidays remaining from this year which I could not take because of the workload, so I want to know whether I can take them during notice period or whether I will get paid for them.
reference: I've some untaken leave — can I use it during my notice, or be paid in lieu?

verbose: Honestly speaking, the main reason I am leaving is the long working hours and the stress, I am not able to spend any time with my family, and my health is also getting affected because of it.
reference: Honestly, the hours and stress have taken their toll — I'm worn out.

verbose: It was a very difficult decision for me to leave, because this was my first job after college and I have learnt so many things here from everybody, and I will always be thankful to all of you.
reference: I've had a good innings — it's my first job, and I've learnt so much here.

verbose: I want to keep in good contact with all of you even after leaving, so please do not hesitate to message me if you need any help with anything related to my old projects in the future also.
reference: Let's keep in touch — do get in touch if anything crops up on my old projects.

verbose: For the exit interview, should I be completely honest about the problems in the team, or is it better to just say positive things only, because I don't want to burn any bridges with anyone here?
reference: How much candour is wise in an exit interview if I don't want to burn bridges?

verbose: So the reason I am resigning is because I am relocating to Scotland with my family, my partner has got a job there, and unfortunately there is no option of working remotely for my role in this team.
reference: We're relocating to Scotland, and remote working isn't viable for this role.

verbose: I am very sorry for giving such a short notice, I know this is not the right way, but due to some sudden personal circumstances I have to leave immediately and I hope you can understand my situation.
reference: I'm terribly sorry for the short notice — personal circumstances mean I have to leave immediately.

verbose: Will the company be able to give me a relieving letter and the experience certificate on my last day itself, because the new company is asking for these documents compulsorily at the time of joining, otherwise they will not let me join?
reference: Is it alright if I have an employment letter on my last day? My new employer needs one.

verbose: I just want to inform everyone that today is my last day in the office, and I want to thank each and every one of you for all your support and help during my four years of working here.
reference: It's my last day — many thanks to you all for four wonderful years.

verbose: I am not leaving because of the money, the new company is actually paying almost the same, it is more because the new role is giving me a chance to work on the climate projects, which I am very passionate about.
reference: It's not the money — it's the chance to spearhead climate projects.

verbose: I would like to request you to please write a reference for me in the future if any company asks you, because you have been my manager for three years and you know my work better than anyone.
reference: Would you mind being a reference in future? You know my work better than anyone.

verbose: I have already discussed with the HR department and they told me that I need to return the laptop and the ID card on my last working day, so I will do that before leaving the office on Friday.
reference: HR say I'll need to hand in my laptop and pass on Friday.

verbose: So I have prepared one document which has all the details about my projects, like what is the current status of each one, what are the pending tasks and who are the main contact people for each project.
reference: I've written a handover document covering each project's status, outstanding tasks and key contacts.

verbose: The most important thing which you have to remember is that the monthly report must be sent to the client by the fifth of every month, otherwise they get very angry and they will call the director directly.
reference: Crucially, the client's monthly report must go out by the fifth, or they escalate to the director.

verbose: There is one client who is a little bit difficult to handle, he is very particular about small things, so please be careful when you are talking to him and always reply to his emails on the same day.
reference: One client's very particular, so mind your p's and q's and reply the same day.

verbose: I will be available on the phone for the first one week after I leave, so if you are having any doubts or any confusion about anything, you can just call me or send me a message, no problem at all.
reference: For my first week away, ring me with any questions — it's no bother.

verbose: All the passwords and the access details for the systems are saved in the shared secure folder, and I have already asked the IT team to give you the access, so it should be done by tomorrow morning.
reference: Credentials are in the secure shared folder, and IT should have your access sorted by tomorrow.

verbose: There are three things which are urgent and must be done this week itself, and the remaining things can wait for some time, so I have marked the urgent things in red colour in the tracker sheet.
reference: Urgent items are red on the tracker; everything else can go on the back burner

verbose: Before I go on leave, let us sit together for one hour tomorrow and I will explain you everything about the project step by step, so that you can ask me whatever questions you are having.
reference: Let's spend an hour tomorrow so I can go over the project and answer questions.

verbose: One thing I forgot to tell you is that the budget for this project is almost finished, there is very little money remaining, so before you approve any new expense please check with the finance team first.
reference: Incidentally, the budget's nearly spent, so check with finance before approving anything.

verbose: While I am on maternity leave, you will be covering my work, and I have already informed all the clients about it, so they will be contacting you directly from next Monday onwards for anything they need.
reference: You'll be filling in for me on maternity leave — clients will contact you from Monday.

verbose: The supplier contract is coming up for renewal next month, and I have already started the negotiation with them, but it is not finished yet, so you will have to continue the discussion from where I left it.
reference: The supplier renewal's due next month; I've started talks, so please pick it up from there.

verbose: There is a small problem with the system which is coming every few days, the report is not generating automatically, so you will have to run it manually until the IT team fixes the problem permanently.
reference: The automated report keeps failing, so make do with running it manually until IT fixes it.

verbose: I have introduced you to all the main stakeholders by email already, and I have told them that you will be the new contact person for this project from now onwards, so they are aware of the change.
reference: I've introduced you to the key stakeholders as their new point of contact.

verbose: If any problem comes which you are not sure how to handle, then please don't take the decision on your own, first discuss with the line manager and then only take any action regarding it.
reference: If you're unsure, run it past our line manager before acting.

verbose: The project is going on track mostly, but there is one risk which I want to tell you about, that the testing phase might get delayed because the vendor has not yet confirmed their dates for the next month.
reference: We're on track, but there's a fly in the ointment: the supplier hasn't confirmed testing dates.

verbose: I have kept all the old files and the documents in a proper order in the shared drive, with the folders for each year, so whenever you want to find something old, you can easily search and find it there.
reference: I've collated the old files on the shared drive by year.

verbose: Please note that the weekly team call is every Tuesday at ten o'clock, and you will be the one running it from next week, so you have to prepare the agenda and send it by Monday evening to everyone.
reference: You'll chair Tuesday's ten o'clock call from next week — agenda round by Monday evening.

verbose: I am handing over this account to you, but I want to tell you honestly that this client is not very happy with us right now, because of the delays in the last quarter, so you have to rebuild the relationship.
reference: Fair warning — this client's unhappy after last quarter's delays, so you'll need to rebuild the rapport.

verbose: The interns who are joining next month will be reporting to you now, instead of me, so please make sure that their training plan is ready before they come, I have already started preparing one draft.
reference: The new interns report to you; I've drafted a plan for their onboarding.

verbose: For the client presentation next Thursday, the slides are almost ready, only the final numbers need to be added, which will come from the finance team by Wednesday, so you will just have to update and send.
reference: Thursday's client deck is nearly done — just drop in finance's figures when they arrive Wednesday.

verbose: I wanted to check with you whether everything is clear in the handover, or whether there is anything you want me to explain once again before I leave, because after Friday it will be difficult to reach me.
reference: Is everything clear, or shall I go through anything again before Friday?

verbose: My advice for you would be that in the first few months in this job, you should focus more on listening and learning how things work, and not try to change everything immediately on the first day itself.
reference: Spend your first months listening and learning — don't put the cart before the horse.
targets: put the cart before the horse

verbose: Whenever you are feeling stuck or confused about anything, whether it is work related or career related, you can always come and talk to me, my door is always open for you, don't hesitate at all.
reference: If you're ever stuck, my door's always open — I'm happy to be a sounding board.

verbose: I think you should apply for that role, even if you feel you are not having all the skills they are asking for, because nobody is having all the skills on the first day, you will learn while doing the job.
reference: I'd be inclined to apply — nobody ticks every box on day one.

verbose: One thing which I learnt very late in my career, and I wish someone had told me earlier, is that building relationships with people is equally important as doing good work, maybe even more important sometimes.
reference: I learnt too late that relationships are indispensable — as important as good work, sometimes more.

verbose: Don't say yes to every single request that comes to you, because then you will be overloaded and the quality of your work will go down, you have to learn to say no politely when it is required.
reference: Learn to say no politely, or you'll bite off more than you can chew.
targets: bite off more than you can chew

verbose: If I were in your place, I would first finish the professional certification which you have started, and only after that I would think about changing the job, because the certificate will give you more options.
reference: If I were you, I'd get the certification done and dusted before moving.

verbose: So tell me, what is it that you really want to achieve in the next two or three years, like what is your actual goal, and then we can work backwards and plan the steps you need to take to reach there.
reference: What's your goal for the next few years? Then we can work backwards and formulate a plan.

verbose: It is completely normal to feel nervous before your first big presentation, everyone feels like that, even I was feeling the same, the only thing is you have to practise many times so that it becomes natural.
reference: Nerves are normal — practise until it's second nature.

verbose: Instead of complaining about the manager to everybody in the office, I would suggest that you go and speak to him directly in a calm way and tell him how you are feeling about the situation.
reference: Rather than complaining to colleagues, grasp the nettle and talk to him calmly.

verbose: You are very talented, and I can see that clearly, but you are not promoting yourself enough, you have to make sure that the right people in the organisation know about the good work you are doing.
reference: You're talented but too modest — don't be afraid to blow your own trumpet.

verbose: One suggestion from my side is that you should find a mentor in the other department also, not only me, because they will give you a different perspective and you will learn about how the other teams work.
reference: It might be worth finding a mentor in another department for a fresh perspective.

verbose: Before you take any big career decision, like leaving a stable job to start your own business, you should first save some money for at least six months of expenses, as a backup in case something goes wrong.
reference: Before going it alone, save six months' expenses as a contingency.

verbose: Don't worry too much about the one mistake which happened in the meeting today, honestly nobody will remember it after one week, everyone makes mistakes, and you handled it very well after that.
reference: It's not the end of the world — and you recovered well.
targets: it's not the end of the world

verbose: What I am noticing is that you are always saying sorry, sorry, sorry in every meeting, even when it is not your mistake at all, and this is making you look less confident in front of the senior people.
reference: You apologise constantly, even when it isn't your fault — it undermines you with senior colleagues.

verbose: My suggestion is that you should start writing some articles or blogs about your work, because that is a very good way to build your profile in the industry and people will start knowing your name.
reference: Writing about your work is a quick win for raising your profile.

verbose: If you are interested in moving into product management, then you should start by volunteering to help the product team in some small projects, so that you will get some exposure and also they will know you.
reference: If product interests you, offer to chip in on small projects to gain exposure.

verbose: So for the interview tomorrow, I would say just be yourself, don't try to give the textbook answers, the interviewers can always see when somebody is just repeating what they have memorised from the internet.
reference: Be yourself — rehearsed textbook answers won't pull the wool over the panel's eyes.
targets: pull the wool over someone's eyes

verbose: Looking at your situation, I feel that you are trying to do too many things at the same time, the job, the course, and the side project, and that is why you are feeling burnt out and tired all the time.
reference: You have a lot on your plate — job, course, side project — no wonder you're exhausted.
targets: have a lot on your plate

verbose: It is good that you are ambitious, but please be patient also, because the promotions in this company usually take two to three years, and if you try to rush it too much it may create a negative impression.
reference: Ambition's great, but promotions here take a few years — more haste, less speed.

verbose: When you go into the negotiation, always remember that you should not say the first number, let them give their number first, and then you can decide whether to go up from there or not.
reference: My rule of thumb in negotiations: never name the first figure.

verbose: I think the feedback which your manager gave you is actually quite fair, even though it is hard to hear, so instead of feeling bad, try to see it as a chance to improve and grow in your role.
reference: It's hard to hear, but it's fair — take it on the chin and grow from it.

verbose: For your first conference talk, my one advice is that don't put too much text on your slides, because nobody will read it, just put one or two key points and a picture, and you speak the rest.
reference: Keep your slides succinct — a key point, an image — and do the rest yourself.

verbose: Whatever you decide, whether you stay in this job or you move to the new one, I will support you, because finally it is your career and your life, and only you can know what is right for you.
reference: Whatever you decide, I'll support you — it's your prerogative.

verbose: You have only been in this team for three weeks, so it is very natural that you don't know everything yet, you are still new, so don't put too much pressure on yourself to know all the answers immediately.
reference: It's early days — three weeks in, nobody expects you to know everything.

verbose: From what you are telling me, it sounds like the job is not right for you, the work is not matching your interests and the culture is not suiting you, so maybe it is time to start looking elsewhere seriously.
reference: It sounds like you're a square peg in a round hole — maybe it's time to look elsewhere.
targets: a square peg in a round hole
